nameStory: The Eastern Screech-Owl gets its name from its haunting, trembling whinny call that sounds like a ghostly scream echoing through the night woods. Despite the name, these owls don't actually screech — they produce a variety of soft trills, whinnies, and hoots that early settlers thought sounded like supernatural screams in the darkness.
description: The Eastern Screech-Owl is a small, stocky owl about the size of a robin, standing roughly 8-10 inches tall. These compact predators have prominent ear tufts that give them a cat-like appearance and large yellow eyes that seem to glow in flashlight beams. They come in two distinct color forms — rusty red or gray — with intricate bark-like patterns that make them masters of camouflage. Their small size and mottled plumage help them blend perfectly against tree bark during the day.

idTips.label: Bark-like camouflage
idTips.description: When pressed against a tree trunk, they look exactly like a broken branch stub with their mottled gray or reddish-brown plumage that mimics bark texture perfectly

idTips.label: Prominent ear tufts
idTips.description: Two pointed feather tufts stick up from their head like tiny horns, giving them an alert, almost cat-like expression when raised

idTips.label: Bright yellow eyes
idTips.description: Large, round yellow eyes that reflect light dramatically at night and seem almost too big for their compact head

idTips.label: Robin-sized body
idTips.description: Compact and stocky, about the size of an American Robin but much rounder and fluffier-looking with their dense feathers

idTips.label: Two color phases
idTips.description: Either warm rusty-red like cinnamon bark or cool gray like weathered wood — both with the same intricate cross-hatched pattern

idTips.label: Trembling call
idTips.description: Soft, musical trill that wavers like a horse's whinny, completely different from the deep hoots most people expect from owls

habitat: Eastern Screech-Owls thrive in mature woodlands with large trees that provide nesting cavities, including oak-hickory forests, mixed deciduous woods, and wooded swamps throughout New England. They're surprisingly adaptable to suburban areas with old shade trees, parks, and even urban neighborhoods as long as there are suitable tree holes for roosting and nesting. Look for them in areas where woods meet open spaces like fields or lawns, which provide hunting grounds for their small prey.

seasonality.spring: Most vocal during breeding season with frequent trilling calls at dusk and dawn. Adults may be seen investigating tree cavities and nest boxes, and you might spot them hunting in the dim light of early morning.
seasonality.summer: Family groups become active as young owls learn to hunt. Listen for begging calls from juveniles and watch for adults carrying prey to nest sites in old woodpecker holes or natural tree cavities.
seasonality.fall: Young owls disperse to find their own territories, making them more likely to be spotted in unusual places. Their calls become more frequent again as they establish winter territories.
seasonality.winter: Often roost in the same tree cavity for days at a time, making them easier to locate if you find their roost site. Their excellent camouflage against bare winter bark makes them nearly invisible during daylight hours.

funFact: Eastern Screech-Owls are such amazing ventriloquists that they can throw their voice to sound like it's coming from a completely different direction, making predators and curious humans search in all the wrong places while the owl watches safely from nearby.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with saw-whet owls, but screech-owls have prominent ear tufts (saw-whets don't) and are noticeably larger. Remember: "Screech has ears that reach" — those pointy tufts are the dead giveaway, even when the owl flattens them against its head when alarmed.
contextualKnowledge: The "screech" name is misleading since these owls rarely make harsh sounds — their calls are actually quite musical and soft. Many people walk right past roosting screech-owls without noticing them because their camouflage is so perfect that they look like a natural part of the tree bark.
compareHints: Eastern Screech-Owls are the only small owls in New England with prominent ear tufts, setting them apart from the similar-sized Northern Saw-whet Owl which has a round head with no tufts. While Great Horned Owls also have ear tufts, they're much larger (hawk-sized versus robin-sized) and have a completely different call pattern. The screech-owl's soft trill is unmistakable compared to the saw-whet's repetitive tooting or the great horned's deep hooting.
